title: Same 10,000 rooms of 23 people. Someone shares YOUR birthday: 569 rooms. Any two share one: 4,922.
description:
The birthday paradox, both questions at once. Ten thousand rooms, twenty three people each, birthdays drawn uniformly from a 365-day year at seed 0 (numpy RandomState). Both panels use the same rooms, the same people and the same birthdays; only the question changes. Top: rooms where someone shares the first person's birthday (yours). Bottom: rooms where any two people share a birthday. People walk in one at a time and both counts update after every arrival.

Measured at seed 0:
- at 23 people: someone shares yours in 569 of 10,000 rooms (5.69%; exact 1 - (364/365)^22 = 5.86%, one standard deviation 0.23 points); any two share in 4,922 rooms (49.22%; exact 50.73%, one standard deviation 0.50 points); ratio 8.65x
- comparisons: you against 22 others; any two among 23 makes 253 pairs
- room 1 on screen: nobody shares yours; two pairs share a birthday, Mar 29 (persons 14 and 20) and Mar 30 (persons 16 and 22); the first pair match arrives with person 20
- the top room keeps filling: 760 rooms at 30 people, 1,250 at 50, 2,383 at 100, 4,231 at 200, 4,986 at 253 (49.86%; exact 49.91%); the smallest crowd with an exact chance over 50% that someone shares yours is 254 people, against 23 for any two
- independent check with 100,000 rooms of 23 at seed 1: 6.00% and 50.65% (exact 5.86% and 50.73%)

Why: your birthday gets one comparison per other person, 22 chances at 1/365 each. Any two people is a comparison for every pair, 253 of them, so the chance of at least one match passes one half already at 23 people. The same one-half for your own birthday needs 253 other people.

The numbers in the narration are the printed outputs of this exact run.

Made end to end by an AI agent: simulation, footage, voice, music, and edit.
